title: Model Evaluation: Choosing, Fairness and Interpretability
oneLiner: Pick a sensible model family, then ask whether it is fair, accountable, transparent, private and secure, and whether people can understand it.

what.html:
Evaluating a model is more than measuring accuracy. This session closes the course with three questions: which kind of model fits my problem; is the model fair and trustworthy; and can people understand why it decides what it decides?

Everyday versionA bank's loan model can be 95% accurate and still be unacceptable if it quietly rejects one community more often, if nobody can explain a rejection to a customer, or if a regulator can't audit it.

why.html:
• Real harm. Hiring tools that penalised the word "women's", cameras that failed to track darker faces, passport checks that misread Asian eyes as closed, and risk scores with unequal error rates are documented cases.
  • Regulation and audits require explanations and accountability.
  • Trust and debugging: an interpretable model tells designers when it learned the wrong thing.

how.title: Start with a model guide
how.html: The scikit-learn cheat-sheet asks a few questions (how much data? predicting a category or a quantity? labelled? text?) and points to an estimator family: classification, regression, clustering or dimensionality reduction. Every branch maps onto a module of this course.

how.title: Five emerging requirements
how.html: Fairness (no gender or ethnic discrimination), accountability (who is responsible when a model fails?), transparency (can it be inspected and comply with regulations?), privacy (protecting users' data, e.g. differential privacy) and security (defending against data poisoning). Together these form the FAccT agenda, which draws on psychology, social science, public policy, statistics and ML.

how.title: Bias is real and measurable
how.html: COMPAS, a commercial risk-assessment tool used on over a million offenders with 137 features, has similar overall accuracy for Black and White defendants but very different false-positive and false-negative rates. Word embeddings trained on text absorb historical gender bias: occupations like "nurse" or "housekeeper" sit close to women, "carpenter" or "mechanic" close to men.

how.title: What fairness means, and why ML can discriminate
how.html: Fairness is the absence of bias toward an individual or a group. Models don't need to be told to discriminate: they approximate patterns in the data, so they learn, and can amplify, the biases in that data.

how.title: Just delete the sensitive column?
how.html: Fairness through unawareness means not using sensitive features (race, gender) directly. It isn't enough: other features act as proxies. In the example, "often goes to Mexican markets" reveals ethnicity, so the model is still discriminatory.

how.title: Limits of unawareness
how.html: Masking sensitive information is hard in practice (it leaks through names, photos, pronouns, postcodes); this is an individual fairness criterion. Datasets can be stereotypical ("the physician hired the secretary because he was overwhelmed") or anti-stereotypical, and models trained on the first kind repeat it.

how.title: Who needs interpretability?
how.html: AI now drives cars, guards security and approves loans. End users need it to trust and understand decisions; regulators for compliance, audits and accountability; model designers to diagnose performance.

how.title: Models that explain themselves
how.html: Decision trees: read the if–then path (tear production rate → astigmatism → age … → hard lenses). Linear regression: each coefficient is one feature's effect. k-NN: show the neighbours that voted (the answer can change between k = 3 and k = 5).

how.title: Fewer features, clearer models: L1
how.html: Adding λΣ|wᵢ| (L1, lasso) to the loss drives many weights to exactly zero, leaving a short model you can read. λΣwᵢ² (L2, ridge) shrinks weights but keeps them all.

how.title: The accuracy–interpretability trade-off
how.html: The most accurate models (deep networks, ensembles) are usually the least interpretable; rule lists and linear models are the reverse. On MNIST, accuracy rose year by year as models became less interpretable. Explainable AI (XAI) aims for both: interpretable-by-design models, post-hoc explanations and hybrid approaches.

demo.html: Walk the cheat-sheet: try "more than 50 samples → category → labelled → under 100K → LinearSVC not working → text" (Naïve Bayes), or "quantity → under 100K → only a few features matter" (Lasso). Each answer names the module where that model was taught.

example.html:
Hiring: a résumé screener that learned to downgrade "women's chess club captain" from past hiring data; the table shows how a proxy feature reintroduces ethnicity.

Contact lenses: a small decision tree that a clinician can read and check.

Supplementary A telecom credit-scoring or fraud model should be audited for disparate impact across regions and languages, and should come with reason codes ("account age < 3 months, 5 SIM swaps") rather than an unexplained score.

misunderstandings: Removing the protected attribute makes a model fair.
Proxies (postcode, shopping habits, names) can reconstruct it.
If overall accuracy is equal across groups, the model is fair.
Error types can differ: COMPAS had similar accuracy but very different false-positive rates.
Interpretable models are always less accurate.
On many tabular problems a well-built sparse linear model or small tree is competitive; the trade-off is a tendency, not a law.
An explanation of a complex model is the model.
Post-hoc explanations are approximations and can be misleading.
takeaways: Use a model guide (data size, task type, labels, text) to choose a starting estimator family.
Beyond accuracy: fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy and security (FAccT).
ML learns and can amplify bias in historical data; equal accuracy can hide unequal error rates.
Fairness through unawareness fails because proxies leak sensitive information.
Trees, linear models (especially sparse L1 models) and k-NN are interpretable; accuracy and interpretability often trade off, which XAI tries to overcome.
thirty: Choosing and evaluating a model involves more than accuracy. A model guide such as scikit-learn's cheat-sheet picks a family from the data size, task type, labels and data type. Then come the FAccT requirements: fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy and security. Models learn patterns, including historical bias, and examples like COMPAS show equal accuracy hiding unequal error rates. Simply removing sensitive features, fairness through unawareness, fails because other features act as proxies. Interpretability serves users, regulators and designers: trees, linear models with L1 sparsity and k-NN explain themselves, while the most accurate models tend to be the least interpretable.
